chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) the second [Imam al-Kazim] regarding a house that belonged to a woman, and she had a son and a daughter. The son disappeared at sea, and the woman died. Her daughter claimed that her mother had designated this house for her, and she had sold parts of it, leaving a portion in the house next to the house of one of our companions. He disliked buying it due to the absence of the son, and feared that it might not be permissible for him to buy it, and no news was known of the son. So he (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Since how long has he been absent?' I said: 'Since many years.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Wait for his absence for ten years, then it may be bought.' I said to him (peace be upon him): 'So if one waits for his absence of ten years, is it permissible to buy it?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'Yes.'

key_terms.غَيْبَة: Absence or disappearance (of a person whose whereabouts are unknown)
key_terms.يَحِلُّ شِرَاؤُهَا: It becomes permissible to buy it
key_terms.يُنْتَظَرُ بِهِ: Wait for him (referring to the period of absence)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on buying property belonging to a missing heir in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) establishes the principle of 'ghaybah' (presumption of absence) for inheritance purposes, ruling that a missing person's estate remains in a state of suspended animation until ten years have elapsed, at which point the uncertainty is lifted. This ruling, found in *Al-Kafi*, provides a practical legal mechanism for resolving property disputes when a heir's status is unknown, balancing the rights of remaining heirs with the potential rights of the missing individual. It reflects the Shia jurisprudential approach of waiting for a definitive period to confirm death or return before finalizing distribution.
